source.title: Stable Minima Cannot Overfit in Univariate ReLU Networks: Generalization by Large Step Sizes
source.authors: Dan Qiao; Kai-Qi Zhang; Esha Singh; Daniel Soudry; Yu-Xiang Wang

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own results and argues that stable, non-interpolating solutions generalize while interpolating solutions can overfit noisy labels, refining when the generalization claim applies.
record.gate_note: The paper studies univariate regression with noisy labels, not arbitrary-label memorization or image classification. It reports learning curves and fitted functions in figures; no exact test-error values are given for these experiments. The width comparison concerns interpolating solutions found by directly optimizing only second-layer weights, not standard gradient training.
record.test_reason: The study establishes generalization bounds and learning-rate effects in univariate noisy regression, but does not test any listed version. Its width illustration uses minimum-norm second-layer least squares and qualitative fitted functions, rather than a test-error comparison for networks trained throughout by gradient descent. Its Hessian curvature measure does not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate but needs the theorem conditions. For univariate two-layer ReLU networks, curvature-constrained stable solutions satisfy weighted total-variation bounds. Under boundedness and interior-support assumptions their generalization gap vanishes; additional optimization, parameter, and target-function assumptions yield a nearly optimal interior MSE rate. A constructed noisy-label example rules out stable interpolation at fixed learning rate for sufficiently large samples. Simulations show learning-rate-dependent smoothness and overfitting.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments use full-batch gradient descent on a two-layer univariate ReLU regression network with fixed design and Gaussian label noise. The width comparison instead directly solves for second-layer weights in interpolating fits. This differs from the listed classification and optimizer studies.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning rate changes fitted complexity and overfitting behavior; increasing learning rate yields smoother fits, while the paper reports overfitting as the learning rate decreases. In the interpolation illustration, changing hidden-neuron count changes the qualitative overfitting regime.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger learning rates produce smoother, sparser fits; sufficiently small learning rates permit fitting noisy labels. Figure 2 describes a U-shaped MSE tradeoff.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning rate implicitly controls function complexity and estimation error in univariate two-layer ReLU regression.

fits_no_version.finding: Minimum-norm interpolating fits move from catastrophic toward tempered overfitting as hidden width increases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing random-feature width can smooth interpolating univariate ReLU regression fits without eliminating overfitting.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorems 4.1–4.4 connect unscaled Hessian curvature to weighted function variation and conditional interior generalization bounds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the stated boundedness and interior-support assumptions, stable univariate ReLU solutions have vanishing generalization gaps; additional optimization and target-class assumptions yield nearly optimal estimation rates.

record.problems: The experiments use one small univariate regression dataset with 30 fixed inputs and show fitted functions and learning curves without exact test-error values or uncertainty estimates. The width illustration uses directly solved interpolating fits rather than standard gradient training.

untested.parts: Natural-label versus random-label classification, near-perfect random-label fitting, and chance-level held-out accuracy.
Held-out error as width increases beyond interpolation for networks trained throughout by gradient descent.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout effects on held-out classification error.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, generalization-gap rankings among comparably fitted convolutional networks, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's arguments about interpolation and flat minima address broader claims than V1–V8. They do not challenge random-label memorization capacity or establish V7's specific sharpness-ranking claim. Qualitative results are readable from the captions; cannot_determine here concerns their ability to establish a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label classification comparison or held-out accuracy at chance is tested.
The width experiment is univariate noisy regression, not MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10, and does not report a numeric test-error sweep past the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classification comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison.
The paper studies Hessian curvature and function smoothness but does not measure magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness or compare generalization-gap rankings with norm- and margin-based measures.
No removal of memorized training examples.

conditions.value: 30 equally spaced fixed design points with noisy labels

rows.note: Authors state that the network barely able to interpolate experiences catastrophic overfitting; the result is qualitative and not standard gradient training.
rows.check: Catastrophic overfitting is explicitly described, but this threshold-width fitted function alone cannot establish V2's post-interpolation test-error trend. Only second-layer weights are fitted by minimum-norm least squares.
